analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal rule barring one company from owning a city's newspaper and its TV or radio stations.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one sponsor and four cosponsors, never got a committee vote and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1975, the FCC has barred a company from owning both a daily newspaper and a broadcast station in the same city, on the theory that a community should not get its news from a single owner. This bill would have ordered the FCC to delete that restriction from its rules within 90 days of enactment, letting newspaper companies buy TV and radio stations and broadcasters buy papers in the same market. It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its telecommunications subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large newspaper publishers and broadcasting companies, which could merge their operations in individual cities, share newsrooms and advertising sales, and gain a bigger share of local advertising dollars.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the FCC to eliminate the provisions of its rule (47 C.F.R. 73.3555) that limit granting or renewing an AM, FM, or TV station license to any company that owns, operates, or controls a daily newspaper, including companies under common control.
The FCC would have had to finish the rule change within 90 days of the bill's enactment, so relief for media companies would have been quick and mandatory rather than discretionary.

analysis.who_pays: Local readers and viewers, who could find a city's main newspaper, television station, and radio stations under common ownership, reducing the number of independent voices reporting on the same community.
analysis.who_pays_short: Readers and viewers in local news markets

drawbacks.text: Eliminating the cross-ownership ban would allow one company to control both a daily newspaper and broadcast stations in the same market, concentrating local news gathering in fewer hands; the existing rule was written to prevent exactly that concentration.

The bill gives the FCC no discretion: it orders the agency to delete the restriction outright within 90 days, bypassing the Commission's usual process for reviewing whether market conditions justify relaxing an ownership rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to companies that want to combine newspapers and broadcast stations in the same city, and they could be real in the form of lower costs and larger advertising packages. But the bill reaches that result by ordering a regulator to delete a consumer-protection rule outright, with no review of what common ownership would mean for local news diversity. The costs fall on audiences that would have fewer independent sources of local reporting.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its telecommunications subcommittee on February 11, 1998, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Klug introduced the bill on February 5, 1998, joined by Reps. Michael Oxley, Ralph Hall of Texas, Cliff Stearns, and Bill Paxon.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce.
On February 11, 1998, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection, where it stayed.
No further action appears in the record; the bill died in subcommittee when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The FCC's newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership ban stayed in place for this Congress, so local markets kept the rule against common newspaper and broadcast ownership; large media companies did not get the merger option the bill offered. With only five sponsors and no committee action, no group spent much to defeat it — it simply never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Local news diversity rules stayed in place

for.name: Rep. Scott Klug
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill ordering the FCC to eliminate the newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership restriction.

for.name: Reps. Michael Oxley, Ralph Hall of Texas, Cliff Stearns, and Bill Paxon
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's four original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Commerce leadership
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Tom Bliley, R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a telecommunications subcommittee on February 11, 1998, and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill got no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and three of the four cosponsors were Republicans; one, Rep. Ralph Hall of Texas, was a Democrat. The bill attracted no visible opposition in the record, only inactivity.

industries.note: Newspaper companies could have bought TV and radio stations, or been bought by them, in the markets where they publish. The bill's benefit to them comes at the cost of fewer independent local news voices for readers.

Station groups could have combined broadcast outlets with daily newspapers in the same city, gaining scale in news gathering and local advertising. Viewers and listeners would have had fewer separately owned local sources.
